kicker: Ember · Science · Week 5 · Tuesday, before the test
title: One rule, three places: volume, pressure and the chain to the end
sub: Do this on Tuesday after “Fix your mistakes”, about 15 minutes. One idea came up wrong in breathing and in gas pressure: what happens to pressure when the space gets bigger. Get it right here and it earns marks in two topics on Wednesday.
skill: The Because Chain (cause, effect, consequence), finished with the quantity the question asks about.
target: AQA Level 3 explanations are “detailed and logically linked”. Your chains stop after the first link. Every chain ends with the thing asked about: “…so the pressure is lower” or “…so air moves in”.

sections.sub: Moments, from memory: two that tripped you up.

blocks.q: You pull the end of a spanner straight along the spanner, away from the nut. Why doesn’t the nut turn?
o: Spanners only work if you push
The line of the force goes through the pivot, so the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero
blocks.why: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot. If the force points straight through the pivot, that distance is 0, so the moment is 0, however hard you pull.

blocks.q: Why is it easier to push a door open at the handle? Which ending gets the last mark?
o: …so a smaller force is needed to make the same moment.
blocks.why: The question asks why it is easier, so end with the force: a smaller force is needed. Finish with the thing asked about.

blocks.html:
One rule: for a fixed amount of gas, bigger volume → lower pressure; smaller volume → higher pressure.

Why: in a bigger space the same particles are more spread out, so they hit each bit of wall less often. Squash them into a smaller space and they hit the walls more often.

Second rule: air moves from higher pressure to lower pressure.

The trap: “more space, more pressure”. It is the other way round.

blocks.q: When you breathe in, the volume of your chest…
o: increases, so the pressure inside decreases
increases, so the pressure inside increases
decreases, so the pressure inside increases
blocks.why: Ribs up and out, diaphragm down: more space. Bigger volume → lower pressure. Now the air outside is at a higher pressure, so air is pushed in.

blocks.q: What does the diaphragm do when you breathe out?
blocks.why: Breathing in: it contracts and flattens (moves down). Breathing out: it relaxes and domes back up, so the chest volume gets smaller and the pressure rises.

blocks.q: You push in the handle of a bike pump with your finger over the end. What happens to the pressure inside?
o: It goes down, because there is less air
It goes up, because the same air is squashed into a smaller volume, so the particles hit the walls more often
blocks.why: No air escapes (your finger is on the end), so the amount of air stays the same. Smaller volume → higher pressure.

blocks.q: A sealed crisp bag puffs up at the top of a mountain. What changed?
o: The pressure inside the bag went up
The pressure outside went down (less air above), so the air inside now pushes out harder than the air outside pushes in
blocks.why: Nothing changed inside the bag at first. Higher up there is less air above you, so atmospheric pressure is lower. Inside is now higher than outside, so the bag is pushed outwards. Look outside the bag, not just inside.

blocks.h: The breathing-in chain, to the end
items: Diaphragm contracts and moves down; rib muscles contract, ribs move up and out
so the volume of the chest increases
so the pressure inside the chest decreases, below the pressure outside
so air is pushed into the lungs from outside, where the pressure is higher
blocks.done: Four links. Most students stop at link 2 and lose the last two marks.

blocks.q: Explain how breathing out pushes air out of the lungs.

points.t: muscles relax: diaphragm moves up, ribs move down and in
so the chest volume decreases and the pressure inside increases (above the pressure outside)
so air is pushed out of the lungs

mark.note: Check the last link: did you end with what happens to the air?

blocks.q: A sealed bag of crisps is taken up a mountain. The bag puffs up. Explain why.
starters: Higher up, the air pressure outside…
so the air inside the bag…

points.t: higher up, atmospheric pressure (outside) is lower: less air above
the air inside the bag now has a higher pressure than the air outside
so the gas pushes the bag outwards (in all directions)

mark.note: Last time you wrote that the pressure inside goes up. Start outside the bag.

blocks.html: If you have 10 more minutes, print the short paper: two chains by hand, then mark them. If not, skip it and rest: the test is tomorrow.

items: Bigger volume → lower pressure. Smaller volume → higher pressure.
Air moves from higher pressure to lower pressure.
Breathing out: the diaphragm relaxes and moves up.
Crisp bag: I started with the pressure outside.
Every chain ended with the thing the question asked about.

blocks.q: “What happens to the pressure in your chest when you breathe in, and why does that make air go in?”
blocks.note: For the parent: listen for “volume goes up, so pressure goes down, lower than outside, so air is pushed in”. If she says “pressure goes up”, ask: “more space or less space for the air?”

paper.title: Science Week 5: volume, pressure and the chain to the end (written)
paper.sub: Ember · Tuesday before the test · about 10 minutes · 7 marks
paper.intro: Skill: the Because Chain. One link per mark. Every chain ends with the thing the question asks about.

blocks.q: 1. Explain how the diaphragm and ribs cause air to move into the lungs.
2. A syringe is sealed at the end so no air can get in or out. The plunger is pulled out, so the air inside has a bigger volume. Explain what happens to the pressure of the air inside the syringe.

selfcheck: Q1: four links, ending with air moving in.
Q2: I said bigger volume → lower pressure, and why (particles hit the walls less often).
Reflection: which link do I usually leave out?

marking.html:
• 1. Diaphragm contracts and moves down / rib (intercostal) muscles contract and ribs move up and out (1); so the volume of the chest increases (1); so the pressure inside the chest decreases, lower than outside (1); so air is pushed (moves) into the lungs (1).
  • 2. The same number of particles in a bigger volume / particles more spread out (1); so they hit the walls less often (1); so the pressure decreases (1).
Score: ____ / 7
